asSun.p: Venus rules Taurus, and The Hierophant is the Taurus card in the tarot, so a Taurus Sun gets it more or less by right. People are sometimes surprised by that pairing, because the picture is a man in heavy robes sitting between two stone pillars with a triple cross in one hand, and Venus is meant to be the pretty planet. But Venus in her own earth sign is about value. What's worth keeping, what's worth paying for, what you'd still want in twenty years. The Hierophant is the card of things that get handed down because somebody decided they were worth it. Taurus is fixed earth, about as settled as a sign gets, and the Sun has no special dignity here, so it takes its colouring from Venus and doesn't fight the sign. Taurus Suns tend to work out who they are slowly, by trying things and keeping the few that hold up, and they're rarely in a hurry about it.

You know what you believe, and you tend to know it before you can explain it. At a work meeting where everyone's excited about the new system, you're the one asking what was wrong with the old one, and quite often you're right to ask. At a family dinner you're the person who remembers how Nan made the gravy and gets a bit precious when someone changes it. You keep the same café, the same barber, the same Sunday walk, and you don't see that as dull. It's how you know who you are. When a friend asks your advice you give an actual answer with reasons attached, and you'd like them to take it. If they don't, you remember.

You make things official for people who need them to be. A friend is thinking about leaving a marriage, or starting a business, or getting sober, and somehow saying it out loud in front of you makes it real. You don't make a speech. You just take it seriously, and that's enough. You're also good at ceremony, and I don't mean churches. You're the one who organises the proper send-off when a colleague retires, who insists on a toast at the barbecue, who still has the birthday cards from 1998. Half the table rolls their eyes at the toast, and they'd be put out if you ever skipped it.

You can confuse your preferences with principles. You like things a certain way, which is fine, but somewhere along the line 'I like it this way' turned into 'this is the right way', and the people around you can feel that shift even when you can't. It shows up over small stuff. How the dishwasher is stacked. Whether a thank-you is a text or a card. What counts as a proper job. There's a bit of Taurus possessiveness in it too. The ideas you hold, you hold the way you'd hold a house, and someone questioning them can feel like trespass. Next time you hear yourself say 'that's just how it's done', stop and ask who taught you that, and whether they'd even still do it that way.

When things go wrong you dig in. The first thing a Taurus Sun does under stress is refuse to move, whether that's refusing to discuss the redundancy, refusing to change the plan, or refusing to leave the house all weekend. A week later you've usually gone rigid about something that isn't the actual problem, the rules at your kid's school, the neighbour's bins, and you're arguing about that with real conviction. The people close to you find this hard, because you go formal and correct and it's very difficult to get past. What helps is slow and physical. A long walk, a job in the shed, your hands in some soil. Once your body has settled you can usually talk about the real thing, and then you're very sensible about it.

You fall slowly, and once you've decided on someone you tend to stay decided for years. Love for a Taurus Sun is something you build and can point to. The flat you did up together, the dog, the savings for the trip, and you're quietly proud of all of it. Scorpio sits opposite Taurus, and the opposite sign is usually what you meet in a partner and have to learn from. For you that's the business of sharing. The joint account, the debt that's both of yours, the decision neither of you gets to make alone. A Taurus Sun can be slow to hand over that kind of ownership, and some of you still say 'my car' and 'my side of the wardrobe' ten years in. Partners notice. Put one thing that's been yours alone into both names.

You're at your best in work that has a lineage to it. A trade learnt from someone who learnt it from someone else, a profession with standards, an institution that's older than you and will still be there after you've gone. You're slow to take a job and slow to leave one, and you tend to end up as the person who knows how everything was set up and why. You also know what your work is worth, and a pay rise that comes late or grudgingly stays with a Taurus Sun for years. Where you get stuck is change that comes down from above with no reason attached. You'll comply on paper and resist in practice, and management notices. If you want a say, get yourself into the room where the decisions are made, and argue for the old way on its merits.

Young Taurus Suns often feel a bit out of step. At twenty your friends are backpacking or changing courses every semester, and you want a steady wage, a car that starts, somewhere of your own, and you're faintly embarrassed about wanting it. Usually you've also taken on your parents' idea of a good life without looking at it closely. By the mid-thirties something tends to test that, a job that folds, a relationship that ends, a house that costs more than it's worth, and Taurus Suns rebuild slowly and far more deliberately the second time. What you keep after that is actually yours. The fifties are often the best of it. The stubbornness has turned into a certainty that doesn't need to argue, and a lot of Taurus Suns take up a craft properly around then, woodwork, bread, a choir, and stick with it for good.

Pick one thing you do because it's how it's always been done. A holiday routine, a work habit, the way you handle money. Ask yourself where it came from and write the answer on the back of an envelope. Then decide, deliberately, to keep it or change it. If you keep it, tell one person why it matters to you. If you change it, do it the new way once and see how it sits. Either way, pick a second thing next month.

asMoon.p: The Moon is exalted in Taurus. In the old language that makes it an honoured guest, treated better there than almost anywhere else in the zodiac, and in plain terms it means your feelings have somewhere solid to land. Taurus is fixed earth ruled by Venus, so what you feel goes through the body first. The smell of a particular kitchen, the weight of a blanket, food that tastes the way it did when you were small. The Hierophant is Taurus's card, and as a Moon card it points at where you go for comfort, which is to things that have been done before. Look at the pair kneeling at the bottom of the picture. They haven't come to invent anything. They've come to be given what the last pair were given, and your sense of safety was built much the same way, out of habits somebody handed you and repeated until your body stopped checking.

You need your rituals and you notice the day one gets skipped. The first coffee made the same way, the call to your mum on a Sunday, the same seat on the train. On a Sunday with nothing planned you don't feel empty, you potter, and by evening you feel mended. When a text arrives that you weren't expecting, bad news or even good news, you usually need a few hours before you can reply properly, because your feelings move at the speed of earth. Moving house is hard on you in a way people underestimate. So is a friend who cancels at the last minute. You're not fragile about it. You just take a while to put things back where they go.

Grief is where you're unusually good, other people's I mean. You don't flinch from it and you don't try to fix it. You turn up at the house with a lasagne, you sit, you come back the next week and the week after that, long after everyone else has gone back to their lives. An exalted Moon has steadiness to spare, and the Hierophant adds something close to a priest's instinct for the rites people need when something ends. You know the funeral matters, the first anniversary matters, the cup of tea at the kitchen table matters, and nobody has to explain why. It shows with smaller losses too. A friend's old dog dies and you're the one who posts a card, and writes more than two lines in it.

You inherited rules about feelings along with the recipes. 'We don't make a fuss.' 'We don't air things outside the family.' 'You're fine, go and wash your face.' Plenty of people with this Moon still follow them without noticing, and a feeling that breaks one gets filed as a failing, so you'll say you're tired when you're actually hurt, or busy when you're lonely. The Moon in Taurus holds on to whatever it was given, and the Hierophant gives the holding a moral flavour. It shows up in comfort as well. Three nights on the couch with the same show and the same takeaway can be restful. Three months of it usually means there's something you haven't looked at. Ask yourself whether you're resting or hiding, and answer honestly.

When you're hurt your first move is to go to ground. You shut the door, you eat what your family ate when someone was ill, you watch something you've seen twelve times. That's the exalted Moon looking after itself, and for a day or two it works. A week on, the danger is that you've sealed the whole thing inside a routine and stopped talking about it, and the people around you can't tell whether you're coping or stuck. Partners find that silence very hard to read, and they often start guessing, badly. The best help is someone who'll come and sit in the routine with you without trying to get you out of it, and then, once you're ready, a slow conversation over food. You tend to open up at a table, with a plate in front of you.

You need to feel held, and I mean that literally. Touch, a hand on the back of your neck, falling asleep in the same position every night. Words matter less to you. What you trust is someone who keeps turning up, same time, same warmth, over months. You're slow to fall and then very hard to shift. The trouble tends to come when a partner needs change and you need continuity. They want to move cities or try a different kind of holiday or rearrange the lounge, and you hear it as a threat to the whole relationship. It usually isn't one. Tell them what you're afraid of losing, specifically, and most of it tends to survive the change.

Your feelings about work are about safety first. You need to know the pay is coming, the desk is yours, the people are the same people next month, and when all that's in place you're remarkably productive and remarkably kind to colleagues. Restructures knock you about far harder than they seem to knock anyone else. You're good in jobs where people come to you upset and need a steady voice, reception, nursing, hospitality, the teacher's aide who knows every kid's name. Keep an eye on how much you take home with you. A Taurus Moon soaks up the mood of a workplace the way soil takes water, and you might not notice until you've been tired for six months.

In your twenties this Moon often clings. To a first love, a hometown, a group of friends, the way your family did things, and moving away from any of it can feel close to physical pain. By the mid-thirties most people with this placement have built their own rituals, their own kitchen, their own version of Christmas, and that's usually a big relief. You find you can keep the warmth of what you came from and drop the parts that hurt. In the fifties you're often the one other people ring when something's gone wrong, the one who holds the family recipes and the family stories, and by then you've usually made peace with keeping them.

Build one small ritual on purpose, one you chose yourself. Something that settles you, a particular tea, a ten-minute walk at dusk, lighting a candle when you get home from work, and do it at the same time every day for a fortnight. When something rattles you during those two weeks, go and do the ritual before you do anything else. Notice how long it takes you to come back to yourself, and whether that gets shorter by the second week.

asRising.p: Your rising sign is the sign that was coming up on the eastern horizon when you were born, and it sets the first house, which is the body and the manner and the way you begin things. With Taurus rising, Venus rules your whole chart, and Taurus's card, The Hierophant, is what people meet first. Have a look at him. He's sitting, and he's in no hurry to get up. That's what strangers pick up about you before you've said much. Taurus is fixed earth, so the first impression is weight and patience, a person who isn't going to be rushed. In whole-sign houses the rest of the chart falls into place around that. Scorpio lands on your seventh house of partners, Aquarius on your tenth of career, and Leo on your fourth of home. Leo and Aquarius both square Taurus and Scorpio opposes it, so the partners, the work and the home you end up with tend to push against that calm front harder than strangers would guess.

It's in how you walk into a room. You don't rush in, you take a look first, and you often end up sitting somewhere comfortable before you've said hello to anyone. At a job interview you come across as more settled than you feel. At a party you tend to find one or two people and stay with them, and they often end up telling you something serious. Strangers ask you for directions. Colleagues assume you've been there for years when it's your second week. And when you start something new, a course, a gym, a hobby, you do it the proper way from the first day, with the right shoes and the right book.

Venus ruling the chart gives the Taurus front a softness people don't expect from something so solid. You tend to have a good eye, a good voice, or good hands, sometimes all three, and you dress and furnish and cook with a sense of what's pleasing that other people notice straight away. That's a real asset in a first meeting. People relax around beauty that isn't showing off. Your pace is catching, too. In a tense meeting, a delayed flight, a waiting room where everyone's on edge, the people near you slow down to match you without knowing they've done it, and the temperature drops a few degrees. I've known nurses and mediators with Taurus rising who reckon that's half the job.

Because you look so steady, people forget to check on you, and you've probably let them. Taurus rising can also be very hard to redirect once it's started down a path, and from outside that reads as calm when it's really a refusal to hear. A colleague suggests a better way at the start of a project and you smile, nod, and carry on exactly as you'd planned. A friend says the restaurant you always pick has gone downhill and you book it again. None of that is dramatic. It builds up though, and people eventually stop suggesting things, which leaves you on your own with your methods a lot of the time.

Your face gives nothing away when things go badly, and that's both the help and the problem. You slow right down. You answer the angry email the next day, you let the argument go quiet, you don't make any sudden moves. If the thing still hasn't been dealt with a week or so later, you've usually planted your feet, and at that point very little moves you, a partner's pleading and a boss's deadline included. It's hard on whoever works or lives nearest. You look normal, so they carry on as normal, and then feel foolish when they find out a month later how bad it was. What helps is a direct question, asked in private by someone you trust. Getting changed helps too, oddly. A shower and clean clothes and you can think again.

Scorpio on your seventh house means the partners who get under your guard are rarely easygoing. You're drawn to intensity, someone private, someone who sees straight through the calm front, and the attraction is often immediate on their side and slow on yours. That's the Taurus and Scorpio axis at work. They want to know what you're really feeling and you'd sooner show them with a home-cooked dinner. Both are ways of loving someone, but it takes a while to learn each other's. Partners also find out, a year or two in, that your easy manner has limits, and they hit them in odd places, like how a Saturday gets spent or which way the couch faces. Say where those limits are early.

With Aquarius on your tenth house, the career you end up in is often stranger than the way you carry yourself. People meet a steady Taurus manner and then find out you work in tech, or community organising, or some odd corner of science, or that you're the one quietly pushing a very old institution to modernise. Aquarius and Taurus square each other, both fixed signs, so there's friction between how you present and where your working life keeps pulling. Used well, that friction makes you persuasive. Colleagues trust a new idea when it comes from someone who looks like they've never done anything rash in their life. Pitch the change in the language of the tradition and it usually gets through.

At twenty, Taurus rising often looks older than it is. You get handed responsibility early because you seem ready for it, and sometimes you are. By the mid-thirties the front has usually become more comfortable to wear, and you've stopped trying to be the most grown-up person in every room. Leo on the fourth house tends to show up around here too. You want a home you're proud of, a place people come to, and a lot of Taurus risings put money and love into a house or a garden in these years. By the fifties the face has caught up with the manner. Venus rules the chart, and you often wear your age well, in a way of dressing that settled decades ago and still works. You might take up something new at sixty, a language or the cello, which surprises anyone who'd assumed you were set in your ways.

Once this week, when someone suggests doing something differently, say yes before your usual pause kicks in. Keep it small. A different route to the shops, a new dish at the restaurant, a colleague's version of the spreadsheet. Pay attention to the moment of resistance, where it sits in your body, and what it feels like to go ahead anyway. You don't need to like the change. Just notice that you got through it fine.

asBirthCard.p: This card comes from your birthdate, and your chart has nothing to do with it. Add every digit of the date together, and if you get a number over 22 add those digits again. If you land on 5, or pass through 23, 32, 41 or 50 on the way, The Hierophant is yours for life, whatever your Sun sign happens to be. Five comes straight after The Emperor, who is four, and four is the square, the table with four legs, rules that stand up by themselves. Five is that structure plus one. Something gets added to the order, a reason, a meaning, a teacher who explains why the rules exist. Straight after five comes The Lovers, card six, which is about choosing. So the Hierophant sits between being told and deciding for yourself, and people with this number tend to spend a long time on that step, some of them quite happily.

People bring you their questions, and they've done that since school. How does this work, what should I do, is this normal. You find yourself explaining things in the staff kitchen, at the pub, in the group chat, often to people who didn't know they'd asked. You care about getting it right, and it bothers you when someone passes on a fact without checking it. You also tend to belong to things, a club, a congregation, a union, a choir, a fan community with its own lore, and you know their history better than most of the members. At a graduation you're the one who notices the bit of the ceremony they skipped this year. You usually say nothing. You notice though.

Fives are translators. You can take something that's been locked up in jargon or ritual or a family's unspoken rules and make it make sense to someone new. That's what the crossed keys at the Hierophant's feet are for on the card, and it's a rarer skill than it sounds. You're the one who explains the in-laws to the new partner, who tells the nervous first-year what the lecturer actually wants, who writes the handover notes nobody else bothers with. Without someone like you, a lot of newcomers would stay on the edge of a group for years, and some of them would quietly leave.

Fives lean on borrowed authority more than they realise. It's easy to reach for 'the rules say' or 'the experts agree' or 'that's what we were taught' when the honest version would be 'I'm not sure'. You can end up defending positions you've never actually tested, and getting sharp with people who ask awkward questions, especially in front of others. It shows up in parenting a lot. The child asks why, and you hear yourself give the answer your own parents gave, word for word. There's also a pull towards gatekeeping, deciding who's in the group and who isn't. Keep an eye out for the moment you feel pleased that someone doesn't belong.

A five in trouble reaches for the structure first. You look up the procedure, you ring the person who knows, you want to do this properly. That helps for a bit. A week later, if the rules haven't fixed it, you can swing hard the other way and throw out the whole framework, the faith, the method, the advice, with a kind of betrayed anger. Friends get whiplash from that, having watched you defend it for years. What actually helps is somewhere in between. Keep the parts of the structure that are still holding you up, the daily walk, the friend from the old group, and put the rest down for a while without deciding anything about it.

Five sits right before The Lovers, and in love that shows. You tend to want a relationship to mean something beyond the two of you, shared values, a family's blessing, some sense that it's recognised by the people who matter. Weddings matter to you more than you'd admit, even if yours was at a registry office. The catch is that you can bring a script into it, what a husband does, what a good girlfriend is like, and hand it to your partner without discussing it. Most of your fights tend to come from that script. Sit down with them at some point and write out what each of you actually expects, the dull stuff included, money and chores and holidays.

Anywhere knowledge gets passed on suits a five. Teaching, obviously, but also training, HR, law, ministry, editing, being the senior tradesperson with an apprentice, being the manager who actually writes things down, the club secretary who's kept the minutes book for twelve years. Fives are good in institutions because you understand why they exist, and you have patience for paperwork that makes other people scream. The trouble is you can stay inside an institution long after it stopped deserving you. Loyalty is part of the number. Every few years it's worth asking whether you still believe in the place or just know your way around it very well.

The pattern at twenty usually goes one way or the other. Either you're devoted to a teaching, a church, a sport, a political line, a guru of some kind, or you're furiously against one. Both are the Hierophant, just facing different ways. By the mid-thirties most fives have had a teacher disappoint them, and that's a real turning point. You start sorting what you were given into what's true and what was only somebody's habit. The fifties tend to be when the number comes into its own. You've become the teacher, often in some informal way nobody gave you a title for, and you're gentler with your students than your own teachers were with you.

Find someone newer than you at something you know well, at work, in a club, in the family, and teach them one thing properly. Take the time to explain why it's done that way as well as how. Then ask them one question about something they know and you don't, and let them teach you back. Pay attention to how it feels to be the student for ten minutes.
